# Don’t let overload protection be the enemy of scaling


[Whatnot Engineering](https://medium.com/@whatnotengineering?source=post_page---byline--7f59abbcb070-----------------------------------------)


8 min read


·


7 hours ago


--


[Marcin Mierzejewski](https://www.linkedin.com/in/marcin-mierzejewski-467183449/) **|** *Reliability Platform (Poland)*


The concurrency limiter in front of our main API at Whatnot has one job: protect the backend from overload. As we scaled, though, it became the component most likely to fall over under a traffic surge. We had grown its Redis fleet from one instance to nine, and the hottest instance still peaked at 92% CPU in load tests. We had even configured that instance to send 60% of its traffic elsewhere, but it still stayed the hottest.


Keeping track of every request was a losing effort. The way out was to stop counting so precisely.


## Concurrency limiting in a nutshell


In short, we limit concurrency rather than rate. We count in-flight requests per request type (GraphQL operation names or REST endpoints), so a request type that slows down gets throttled harder.


Why count requests in flight instead of requests per second? The number in flight is roughly the arrival rate times how long each request takes. If a database query slows from, say, 50 ms to 500 ms, the same traffic keeps ten times as many requests in flight. Each one holds a worker and a database connection while it waits, so the pile-up slows everything else down, which makes requests slower still.

A rate limiter doesn’t notice, because the request rate hasn’t changed. A concurrency limiter does. The slow request type hits its cap on in-flight requests, and the extras get a fast 503 instead of joining the queue. That request type sheds load early, and the rest of the API keeps its workers and connections. A separate per-IP cap stops any one client from taking more than its share. For simplicity, we’ll only talk about request-type concurrency limiting, unless stated otherwise.


## How the limiter became the bottleneck


In 2024, my colleague Karol Gil wrote about[how we initially built the limiter](https://medium.com/whatnot-engineering/expecting-the-unexpected-managing-3x-traffic-surges-at-whatnot-c8c3d3f76891) . That design worked, and a few weeks later it throttled a query storm that nearly tripled request volume. However, it paid for a precise, synchronous count on every request. Each API request made 4 calls to a Redis primary (acquire and release, for the request type and IP), and each key’s count was kept as two 30-second windows, the current one and the previous one. Each call ran a Lua script that read and updated both windows atomically. That’s up to 12 operations per request, all on the primary that owned the key.


Two things made that expensive to scale. First, none of those operations could go to a replica, so every new request per second landed on the primaries up to 12 times over, and the only way to add capacity was to add primaries. Second, adding primaries wasn’t the answer to hot keys. We routed operations based on request type only, so all the traffic for a request type landed on one instance. Adding an instance changed which request types shared a node, but that was luck: it could separate two hot ones or put them together.


We kept adding primaries anyway, going from one instance in mid-2024 to nine by September 2025, and every load test still kept finding one above 80% CPU. Meanwhile, Black Friday was a few months away, and we expected it to bring triple our highest peak so far. On top of that, each addition came with an operational cost as well — a Terraform change, new connection URLs in the environment variables, and a rollout of the whole fleet. This dance had already caused two incidents before.


## Ideas that didn’t work


The key constraint is how thin our traffic is per process. At the time, the API ran on 3,000 to 7,000 pods, so each process saw about 5 requests per second at peak. Here’s what we considered:


- **Local-only limiting.** At 5 requests per second, a pod can’t tell an overload from noise.
- **Sticky routing.** It makes local counts meaningful, but trades hot Redis keys for hot pods.
- **Rate limiting.** It’s simpler, but it loses the signal we care about most: requests getting heavier.
- **Random sampling.** Counting only a sample of requests would cut Redis load, but it adds config to maintain. Our limits were static and already needed updating week by week as traffic grew. Sampling would have meant even more manual tuning.
- **The same design on Redis Cluster.** Sharding gets automated, but every call still hits a primary, and the Lua script needs both windows on one node. Hot keys stay hot.
- **One Redis per availability zone.** Three times the scaling toil, and it only delays the hot partitions.
- **A proxy in front of the API.** Probably the right long-term home, but a year-long project at the time. We had a few months before Black Friday.


We needed something that kept the core semantics, fit inside the existing architecture, and scaled horizontally.


## Eventual consistency to the rescue


To scale further, we had to question why a concurrency limiter needed an exact, real-time count at all. The overloads we care about build up over seconds as slow requests pile up, not in milliseconds. A count that lags by 100 ms still catches a slow endpoint long before workers run out. It can miss floods of very short requests, but catching those was never the concurrency limiter’s job.


In return, we no longer need the primary on every request:


- **Concurrency** **checks** **go to replicas** , since slightly stale reads are allowed. Each shard can add up to 5 of them as read traffic grows. And a plain GET gets the job done, no need for a Lua script.
- **Updates** **are** **batched.** Since a delay in recording a request is allowed, each pod folds many increments and decrements into a single value per key and batch the writes periodically. INCRBY per key is enough, which is easier on the primary than a Lua script. On top of that, write load on the primaries now scales mostly with the number of API pods, each sending one batch per sync interval, rather than with every request. Since each pod handles a low RPS, each batch touches only a handful of keys.
- **Windows can live on different shards.** A key’s current and previous window counters no longer have to sit on the same node. This allows routing by request type and window timestamp (keys look like ds:<key>:<window_start_ms>), so each new window lands on an effectively random shard. A hot key still loads one or two shards at any moment, but it moves every window, so a hot partition, or two hot keys colliding, is likely short-lived. As a bonus, losing a shard costs one window of a key, not the whole key.

This removes both factors that made the old limiter expensive to scale: every operation landing on a primary and hot keys pinning one node.


## The eventually consistent distributed semaphore


This is how the successor of the initial concurrency limiter puts these ideas into practice with three operations:


- **Acquire.** GET the current and previous window for the request type from replicas. If their sum is below the limit, add +1 to a local, in-process delta and let the request through. Otherwise, reject it: 503 if the request type is over its limit, 429 if the IP is.
- **Release.** Add −1 to the local delta. Omits Redis entirely. If the pod dies before its next sync, the decrement is lost and the count stays too high until that window ages out.
- **Sync.** Every 100 ms, a background task in each process flushes its local deltas to the primaries as one pipelined batch of INCRBYs. Once the batch is written, the sent amounts are subtracted from each key’s local delta, so changes made during the flush carry over to the next one.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


We also stopped setting TTLs. A window counter is dead after 60 seconds, so the old limiter ran PEXPIRE on the Redis main thread for every request type and IP in every window, while more than 99% of Redis memory sat empty. Now we set no TTL at all and let Redis’s LRU eviction clean up old windows when memory actually fills up.


What do the numbers say? In the final load test before Black Friday 2025, the old limiter’s hottest Redis instance passed 90% CPU, a few others came close, and all nine primaries went above 80%. On 8 shards, the semaphore’s hottest primary barely touched 50% at peak. It also delivered on the scalability promise. A year later, after a few adjustments to its Redis cluster topology, it’s still one of our main protections against overload. In load tests ahead of Black Friday 2026, it handles 4x the traffic that would overwhelm the old limiter, with plenty of headroom left.


## The tradeoff we accepted


The old limiter chose consistency: every acquire and release went synchronously through the one counter that owned the key, or failed open. The new one chooses availability. Each pod works from an approximation that can be one sync interval plus replication lag behind.


That lag is behind the blind spot for very short requests mentioned earlier. A request that starts and finishes between two syncs never reaches Redis, so however many of them there are, the limiter never sees them.


We accepted that on a bet: short requests are cheap. What hurts the backend is requests getting slow, and once a request type slows down, its requests span a sync and get counted.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


## Next up: Adaptive Concurrency Controller


Both limiters so far share one weakness: their limits are static. With the app growing as fast as it does, new endpoints ship and existing ones see more traffic all the time, so keeping those numbers right is a constant operational tax. And during a big event, when traffic and latency shift by the minute, there’s no realistic way to retune them on the spot.


That’s why our next step is an adaptive concurrency controller. Instead of reading a fixed limit from config, it automatically adjusts each request type’s limit based on how the backend is actually behaving. Stay tuned for a future post!
